title: New York’s Mayor Needs To Do More Than Eliminate ‘Gifted’ Programs
author: Natalie Wexler
summary: Natalie Wexler argues that New York City's plan to replace gifted-and-talented classes with Brilliant NYC will not make the system fairer unless reading instruction itself changes. She agrees that tracking four-year-olds by test makes little sense but locates the real inequity in how schools teach reading: too little systematic phonics, and comprehension taught as skills and strategies rather than by building academic knowledge. Children from educated families pick that knowledge up at home while others depend on schools that rarely supply it. She recommends a knowledge-building elementary literacy curriculum with strong teacher training and decoding-focused dyslexia screening. It sits in Learning & Curriculum because the argument is about literacy instruction and curriculum content.
points: Ending gifted programs achieves little unless the underlying approach to reading instruction changes.
Many children need systematic phonics, and screening should test decoding separately from comprehension.
Teaching comprehension as skills like finding the main idea displaces the academic knowledge that makes reading comprehensible.
Children without knowledge-rich homes depend on schools for background knowledge, and low-scoring schools are least likely to build it.
A content-rich curriculum covering science, social studies and the arts, with teacher training, is the fairest step New York could take.
quotes: At least one aspect of the plan makes sense: kids shouldn’t be tracked on the basis of a standardized test taken at age four, unless they’re off-the-charts prodigies—and perhaps not even then. And a large-scale study has found that gifted-and-talented programs generally have little effect on achievement, although the programs vary so much it’s hard to say whether that’s a reliable finding.

And “reading” is the crux of the problem. The way schools in New York City and most other places in the United States approach reading instruction ends up stifling the potential of untold numbers of children. One reason is that educators have long underestimated how many kids need systematic instruction in phonics in order to fluently decipher words.

Some kids are able to acquire that kind of knowledge at home, usually because they have more highly educated parents, while others rely on school for that—and, in our current system, those kids are often the least likely to get it there. Schools with low test scores are the most apt to focus on comprehension skills at the expense of building knowledge, in a futile effort to boost scores.

The best thing New York could do to make its school system fairer would be to adopt one of the knowledge-building elementary literacy curricula that are now available, and provide teachers with high-quality training in how to implement it. But that seems highly unlikely.

If the screening is focused on things like kids’ ability to sound out discrete words, including nonsense words that conform to phonics patterns that have been taught, it could catch “decoding” problems and help put students on the path to success. Similar screening tests have been adopted in England and parts of Australia and appear to be working well.

There’s a lot of potential brilliance among the underserved students of New York City, and in many other places, that is currently being nipped in the bud. But eliminating gifted and talented classes falls far short of what is needed to allow it to blossom.
